titre: A fake Mumm on a bottle, and a federal law that collapses
accroche: In 1879, the Supreme Court rules that a trademark is neither an invention nor a work, and strips Congress of the foundation it chose to protect it.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1876, the U.S. Congress passes a criminal law to punish trademark counterfeiting. In lower Manhattan, two merchants, Steffens and Wittemann, are prosecuted for selling fake champagne under the labels of G. H. Mumm & Co. and of the private brand of Kunkleman & Co., known as “Piper Heidsick,” two houses of Reims. In Ohio, a third, Johnson, is prosecuted for imitating the “O K” mark, registered for whisky packaging by Charles F. O'Donnell. The judges of the New York and Ohio circuits disagree on the constitutionality of the 1876 law and refer the question to the Supreme Court.

## A trademark is neither an invention nor a work

The 1876 law builds on an earlier one, from 1870, by which Congress had organized the federal registration of trademarks. To ground that power, Congress had relied on the same constitutional clause as patents and copyright: Article I, Section 8, Clause 8, which lets it secure “for limited times” to authors and inventors the exclusive right to their writings and discoveries.

On November 17, 1879, the Supreme Court, in an opinion by Justice Samuel Freeman Miller, rejects that foundation. A trademark, the Court writes, does not presuppose originality, invention, discovery, science or art. It may consist of a word already known, a picture already seen, a symbol already used elsewhere: nothing is created. “It is simply founded on priority of appropriation”: it rests only on having been the first to adopt it in trade. The clause that authorizes Congress to reward creation therefore cannot ground a right that rewards only earlier use.

The Court also declines to save the law through the commerce clause: the 1876 text does not limit its application to commerce between the states or with foreign nations, the only commerce that clause allows Congress to regulate, and the Court refuses to rewrite a criminal law itself to make it valid. Both laws fall: the Court answers the questions certified by the circuits in the negative, and sends the three cases back.

## Two rights, two separate foundations

Congress has to start over. It passes the Trade Mark Act of 1881, based this time on the commerce clause, but drafted so cautiously that it covers only marks used in trade with foreign nations and with Native American tribes. It takes a law of 1905 to enact general protection for marks used within U.S. territory, still on that same basis.

The episode fixes a separation American law has kept ever since: patents and copyright rest on the clause that rewards creation, trademarks on the one that governs commerce. A common intuition files all three rights under one label, “intellectual property”; in 1879, the Court gave them two distinct constitutional foundations. It does not, however, settle the broader question of the link between a trademark and commerce in general: it expressly leaves it open, and it is on the commerce clause, carefully circumscribed, that Congress will rebuild protection.

citation.texte: It is simply founded on priority of appropriation.
citation.source: Trade-Mark Cases, 100 U.S. 82, opinion of the Court, November 17, 1879

carte.punch: A champagne trademark brought down the first federal trademark law in the United States.
carte.idee: In 1879, the Supreme Court rules that Congress had based its 1870 trademark law on the same clause as patents and copyright, when a trademark requires neither invention nor work, only priority of use. The law falls, and Congress has to start again from a different clause.

quiz.question: On what constitutional basis had Congress built the 1870 federal trademark law, and why does the Supreme Court find it insufficient in 1879?
choix: On the commerce clause, which the Court finds too narrowly drafted to cover purely local trade
On the Tenth Amendment, which the Court finds reserved to the states alone in matters of property
On the Supremacy Clause, which the Court finds inapplicable to a federal criminal law
On the same clause as patents and copyright, which presupposes a creation, whereas a trademark rests only on priority of use
quiz.explication: Congress had modeled the 1870 law on the clause that grounds patents and copyright (Art. I, §8, cl. 8), which presupposes an invention or a work. The Court finds that a trademark requires neither: it arises from priority of use alone, which that clause does not protect.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which champagne brands are at the heart of the prosecutions of Steffens and Wittemann?
choix: G. H. Mumm & Co. and the brand known as “Piper Heidsick”
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The two merchants are prosecuted for selling fake champagne under the labels of G. H. Mumm & Co. and of the private brand of Kunkleman & Co., known as “Piper Heidsick.”

quiz_supplementaire.question: What law does Congress pass in 1881 to replace the one struck down in 1879, and on what basis?
choix: A law based on the Tenth Amendment, leaving each state to regulate trademarks
The Trade Mark Act, based on the commerce clause, limited to foreign and Native American trade
An international treaty signed with France to protect champagne brands
A new law based on the same clause as patents, but drafted more broadly
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Congress passes the Trade Mark Act of 1881, based this time on the commerce clause, but cautiously limited to trade with foreign nations and with Native American tribes.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why does the Court also refuse to save the 1876 law through the commerce clause?
choix: Because the merchants prosecuted lived outside the United States
Because the commerce clause concerns only agricultural goods
Because the text does not limit its application to commerce between the states or with foreign nations
Because Congress had no power to legislate on criminal matters
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The 1876 text does not limit its application to interstate or foreign commerce, the only commerce that clause allows Congress to regulate, and the Court refuses to rewrite a criminal law.
